units.title: Unit 1 - Introducing Anthropology and Its Subject Matter

sections.heading: What anthropology studies
paragraphs: Anthropology is the holistic and comparative study of humanity. It examines people as biological and cultural beings who live in societies and interact with one another and with their environments across time and space.

The word comes from Greek roots meaning human beings and the study of. Anthropology asks how humans are similar and different, how ways of life develop, and how biology, culture, society, language and environment interact.

sections.heading: Scope and core perspectives
bullets: Holism studies a topic in relation to connected parts of human life rather than isolating one feature.
Comparison examines similarities and differences across communities, historical periods and settings; it helps avoid treating one’s own experience as universal.
The cultural perspective considers learned and shared meanings and practices. The biological perspective examines human evolution, variation and adaptation.
Fieldwork and contextual study help anthropologists understand practices from the perspectives of the people involved, while comparison links local experience to wider patterns.
Anthropology includes the study of contemporary peoples and the archaeological and biological evidence of earlier human life.

sections.heading: History, misconceptions and related disciplines
bullets: The discipline developed through changing intellectual and colonial histories; modern anthropology critically examines how earlier theories and research practices were shaped by unequal power relations.
Anthropology is not limited to studying distant or ‘primitive’ societies, bones, fossils or curiosities. It studies all humanity, including familiar communities and contemporary institutions.

It overlaps with sociology, history, psychology, biology, linguistics, political science and economics, but its holistic, comparative and field-based attention to human diversity gives it a distinctive combination of approaches.
Anthropology contributes to understanding social issues, cultural differences, development, health, education, heritage and communication across communities.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Define anthropology and explain the meaning of holism and comparison.
Distinguish anthropology from a narrow study of only one society or one aspect of humanity.
Explain one way anthropological knowledge can be useful in public or professional life.

sections.heading: Archaeological anthropology
paragraphs: Archaeological anthropology studies past human societies through material remains such as tools, settlement patterns, buildings, food remains and artifacts. Context and association matter: an object’s location and relationship to other evidence help establish how it was used and what it can support about past life.

sections.heading: Linguistic anthropology
paragraphs: Linguistic anthropology studies language in social and cultural contexts: how people communicate, how language varies and changes, and how speech relates to identity, power, knowledge and social relationships.

sections.heading: Socio-cultural anthropology
paragraphs: Socio-cultural anthropology examines contemporary social life, institutions, relationships, beliefs, values and practices. Participant observation, interviews and other ethnographic methods help researchers understand both everyday action and the meanings people give it.

sections.heading: Physical or biological anthropology
paragraphs: Biological anthropology studies human evolution, biological variation, adaptation, primates, fossils and human biology. It connects evidence about the body and evolutionary history with environmental and cultural contexts.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Match each sub-field to its main evidence and questions.
Give an example of how two sub-fields might study different aspects of the same community or historical issue.
Explain why archaeological evidence must be interpreted in context.

topics.title: Human origins, variation and the concept of race

sections.heading: Evolutionary and paleoanthropological perspectives
bullets: Human origins are studied using multiple forms of evidence, including fossils, comparative anatomy, genetics, archaeology and the dating of remains.
Human evolution is a branching process rather than a simple ladder from ‘less advanced’ to ‘more advanced.’ Different hominin populations lived at different times and some overlapped.
Biological traits such as bipedalism, changes in teeth and jaws, and brain development are interpreted alongside evidence of behavior, technology and culture.
Human beings combine biological capacities with learned cultural knowledge; neither biology nor culture alone explains the full range of human adaptation.

sections.heading: Human biological diversity and race
bullets: Human physical variation exists, but traits vary across populations and do not sort humanity into a small set of discrete, internally uniform biological races.
The module critiques historical racial typing: classifications often selected visible traits, imposed rigid boundaries on gradual variation and reflected social and political assumptions.

Race remains socially consequential because people and institutions assign meaning to categories and distribute opportunities or discrimination through them; this social reality is distinct from treating race as a fixed biological taxonomy.
Anthropological accounts distinguish shared human ancestry and species membership from variation shaped by population history, environment, migration and gene flow.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Explain why human evolution is described as branching rather than a straight-line progression.
Distinguish biological human variation from historically constructed racial categories.
Describe how biological and cultural evidence can complement one another in studying human life.

units.title: Unit 3 - Human Culture and Ties That Connect Society

sections.heading: Understanding culture
paragraphs: Culture is learned and shared knowledge, meanings, values, norms and practices through which people organize life. It includes material products as well as non-material ideas and relationships; it is not simply refinement, art or a list of customs.

sections.heading: Key characteristics and elements
bullets: Culture is learned through socialization and enculturation rather than inherited only through genes.
It is shared but not perfectly uniform: people may interpret, negotiate or contest norms differently by generation, gender, class, locality or personal experience.
Culture is symbolic, integrated across domains, transmitted between generations and capable of change.
Material culture includes tools, houses, clothing, food and technologies. Non-material culture includes language, beliefs, values, norms, knowledge and institutions.
Cultural universals are features found across human societies; generalities are common but not universal patterns; particularities are distinctive features of specific societies.

sections.heading: Ethnocentrism, relativism and human rights
bullets: Ethnocentrism judges other ways of life by the standards of one’s own culture, often treating those standards as naturally superior.

Cultural relativism seeks to understand practices in their cultural and historical context before judging them. It is a method of understanding, not an instruction to excuse harm or abandon ethical analysis.
Anthropologists can combine contextual understanding with careful consideration of human rights, power, disagreement and the experiences of affected people.

Culture changes through innovation, migration, diffusion, contact, economic and political change, and the choices people make. Change is not simply loss or replacement; older and newer practices may coexist and be reinterpreted.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Distinguish material from non-material culture and provide examples.
Compare ethnocentrism with cultural relativism while explaining their relationship to human-rights questions.
Identify a mechanism of culture change and describe its effects without assuming cultures are static.

topics.title: Marriage, family, kinship and culture areas

sections.heading: Marriage and family
bullets: Marriage is a socially recognized relationship whose meaning, rules and obligations vary across societies and historical settings. Anthropological comparison asks what relationships and rights the institution organizes in each context.
Family is a social institution of relatedness, care, residence, reproduction and resource sharing; its forms are diverse and are not limited to one household model.

Marriage and family relationships can connect households, establish alliances, allocate responsibilities and shape inheritance or social identity. Avoid assuming that one local arrangement is universal.

sections.heading: Kinship and descent
bullets: Kinship refers to culturally recognized relationships created through descent, marriage, adoption and other forms of social connection.
Descent systems organize group membership and relationships across generations. A society may emphasize lines traced through mothers, fathers, both sides, or other culturally defined relations.
Kinship terminology classifies relatives and can reveal how a society organizes duties, respect, inheritance, residence and social identity.

sections.heading: Culture areas and contact in Ethiopia
bullets: The module uses culture-area examples such as plough-based farming, enset cultivation and pastoral livelihoods to illustrate relationships among ecology, subsistence, mobility and cultural practices.
A culture area is an analytical way to discuss shared patterns in a region; it does not mean every person in that area has an identical culture.
Trade, migration, intermarriage, conflict, cooperation and shared institutions create cultural contact and historical interaction among communities.
Ecological adaptation shapes livelihoods but does not mechanically determine culture; history, social organization, technology and human choices also matter.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Define kinship and descent and explain why family forms vary.
Compare the plough, enset and pastoral culture-area examples while avoiding stereotypes about individuals.
Explain how culture contact can produce exchange, change and shared practices.

units.title: Unit 4 - Marginalized, Minorities and Vulnerable Groups

sections.heading: Core concepts
bullets: Marginalization is a process through which individuals or groups are pushed to the social, economic or political edges and face reduced access to resources, recognition, participation or decision-making.

A minority is not defined only by population size; a group may be numerically large and still face exclusion, or numerically small without being marginalized. Power and access are central to analysis.
Vulnerability describes heightened exposure to harm or barriers in a particular context. It is shaped by institutions and conditions, not an inherent defect of the people affected.
Intersectionality helps examine how categories such as gender, age, disability, ethnicity, religion, occupation and class can combine to shape people’s experiences.

sections.heading: Forms discussed in the module
bullets: Gender-based marginalization can restrict participation, resources, safety and decision-making for women and girls, including through harmful practices and gender-based violence.
Occupational marginalization can stigmatize groups whose livelihoods or inherited work are treated as lower status, limiting social recognition and opportunity.
Children and older persons may face age-based vulnerability when services, decision-making or protections fail to account for their needs and rights.
Religious and ethnic minorities can face exclusion when their identities, practices or access to public life are not respected.
People with disabilities may face barriers created by inaccessible buildings, services, communication and attitudes; inclusion requires changing environments as well as addressing individual needs.

sections.heading: Human rights and anthropological approaches
bullets: Human-rights frameworks affirm equal dignity, protection and participation. The unit refers to instruments such as the Convention on the Rights of the Child and CEDAW as frameworks addressing discrimination and rights.
Anthropological analysis asks how broad rights principles are experienced in local contexts, how power operates, and whose voices are included in decisions.
Inclusive practice means removing barriers, ensuring equal access and participation, and recognizing the knowledge and agency of affected groups.
Description should avoid treating a marginalized group as homogeneous or speaking about people only as passive victims; attend to variation, resistance and leadership within groups.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Distinguish minority status from marginalization and explain the role of power.
Give examples of structural barriers and suggest an inclusive response.
Explain how human-rights principles and local context can both inform anthropological analysis.

units.title: Unit 5 - Inter-Ethnic Relations, Identity and Multiculturalism

sections.heading: Concepts of ethnicity
paragraphs: Ethnicity refers to a socially meaningful sense of group identity connected to ideas of shared history, ancestry, language, culture or collective experience. Which features matter and how they are interpreted can change across contexts.

sections.heading: Identification and categorization
bullets: Identity can be self-ascribed (how people identify themselves) and externally ascribed (how others or institutions categorize them). These may agree or conflict.
Ethnic boundaries are produced and maintained through interaction, symbols, narratives, institutions and distinctions between ‘us’ and ‘them.’ Boundaries can be emphasized, negotiated or crossed.
Ethnicity is not simply the sum of cultural traits. People may share practices across group lines while maintaining distinct identities, or identify with a group despite internal cultural diversity.
Historical overview helps explain how administrative systems, migration, political change and collective memory shape ethnic categories and relations.

sections.heading: Three theoretical approaches
bullets: Primordialism emphasizes deep, inherited or emotionally powerful attachments, often associated with kinship, ancestry, language or shared history.
Instrumentalism views ethnicity as a resource or basis for mobilization that people and leaders may use strategically in pursuit of political, economic or social goals.
Social constructivism emphasizes that ethnic identities and boundaries are historically produced and continuously shaped through social interaction, institutions and changing circumstances.
These approaches highlight different dimensions; compare their assumptions rather than treating one short description as a complete explanation of every case.

sections.heading: Multiculturalism and inter-ethnic relations
bullets: Multiculturalism recognizes the presence and public participation of diverse cultural and ethnic communities within a shared society.
Inter-ethnic relations include cooperation, exchange, shared institutions, negotiation, competition and conflict; outcomes depend on historical and political contexts.
Inclusive relations require equal citizenship and participation while allowing communities to maintain meaningful identities and practices.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Distinguish self-identification from external categorization.
Compare primordialist, instrumentalist and constructivist accounts of ethnicity.
Use a contextual example to explain how ethnic identity can be meaningful and changeable at the same time.

units.title: Unit 6 - Customary and Local Governance Systems and Peacemaking

sections.heading: Local governance
paragraphs: Indigenous and local governance systems are community-rooted ways of organizing authority, responsibilities, decision-making and social order. Their institutions may include elders, councils, customary leaders and community assemblies, with legitimacy grounded in locally recognized histories and practices.

sections.heading: Conflict resolution and peacemaking
bullets: Customary institutions may use dialogue, mediation, elders’ deliberation, public acknowledgment, apology, compensation, reconciliation rituals or community agreements.

Intra-ethnic institutions address disputes within a community; inter-ethnic mechanisms involve parties from different groups and may require recognized intermediaries or agreements across communities.
A process often aims not only to decide who is right but also to restore relationships, reduce retaliation and reintegrate parties into social life.
Examples in the module include institutions such as Gadaa, Xeer, Siqqee and women-led peacemaking practices including Don Kachel; their procedures and authority differ by community and context.
Women can gather information, mediate, mobilize networks and lead reconciliation. Their contributions may be overlooked when governance is described only through male-dominated formal offices.

sections.heading: Legal pluralism
bullets: Legal pluralism describes the coexistence and interaction of customary, religious and state legal orders in a society.
People may draw on more than one system in resolving a dispute; systems can cooperate, compete or produce conflicting rules and outcomes.
Analysis should consider recognition, jurisdiction, rights protections, accessibility, gender and power, and whether affected people can participate meaningfully.
Respect for local institutions can be considered alongside constitutional and human-rights commitments; neither local practice nor state law should be assumed to operate uniformly in every case.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Distinguish intra-ethnic from inter-ethnic conflict resolution.
Explain how customary mechanisms may combine mediation, compensation and restoration of relationships.
Define legal pluralism and discuss one possible benefit and one challenge of multiple legal systems.

topics.title: Meaning, features, value and domains of indigenous knowledge

sections.heading: Definition and characteristics
paragraphs: Indigenous knowledge systems are locally developed and transmitted bodies of experience, understanding, values, skills, practices, technologies and institutions. They are generated through long interaction with social and physical environments and are adapted to local conditions.

sections.heading: Features and significance
bullets: Knowledge is often transmitted through practice, oral teaching, observation, apprenticeship, community institutions and intergenerational exchange.
It is dynamic rather than frozen: people test, adapt, combine and sometimes abandon practices as circumstances change.
Indigenous knowledge can contribute to livelihoods, food security, healthcare, environmental stewardship, social protection, governance and conflict resolution.
Knowledge is diverse within communities; age, gender, occupation, experience and access can shape who holds or transmits particular knowledge.
Documentation and use should address consent, attribution, ownership, benefit sharing and the risk of extracting knowledge without respecting the communities that sustain it.

sections.heading: Domains and connections
bullets: Agricultural knowledge may include crop varieties, soils, livestock, planting calendars, storage and local adaptation to weather.
Medicinal knowledge includes human and veterinary practices and may inform research, while requiring careful evaluation of safety and evidence.
Ecological knowledge concerns relationships among species, land, water, climate and resource management; it supports local environmental decision-making.
Other domains include climate and weather patterns, social organization and mutual aid, customary governance, peace and security, and technologies.
Domains are interconnected: ecological knowledge can support agriculture and health, while institutions shape how resources and expertise are shared.

sections.heading: Challenges and preservation
bullets: Challenges include loss of languages and transmission pathways, stigma, displacement, environmental change, unequal power, commercialization and insufficient recognition.
Preservation is not only archiving. It includes supporting practitioners, languages, land and institutions, intergenerational learning, community control and respectful collaboration.
Knowledge systems can complement scientific inquiry, but claims and methods should be assessed carefully and contextually rather than romanticized or dismissed in advance.

sections.heading: Final exam review
bullets: Define indigenous knowledge systems and identify several connected domains.
Explain why indigenous knowledge is dynamic, locally grounded and socially transmitted.
Discuss both the value of preservation and ethical challenges in documenting or applying community knowledge.
